exam.name: NCMHCE
exam.whyThisModuleMatters: This module trains learners to recognize diagnostic patterns in case vignettes, rule out competing diagnoses, apply duration and severity requirements, and distinguish primary diagnoses from specifiers and differential diagnoses.

intro.summary: This module covers major DSM-5-TR diagnostic categories tested on the NCMHCE. The focus is not memorizing labels in isolation. The focus is learning how symptoms, duration, impairment, exclusion rules, and differential diagnosis appear in clinical cases.
learningObjectives: Recognize hallmark symptoms of major DSM-5-TR disorders
Apply duration and symptom-count rules when diagnosing from a vignette
Differentiate closely related disorders using rule-out reasoning
Distinguish diagnoses from specifiers, severity levels, and associated features
Identify when medical conditions, substances, bipolar disorders, psychosis, or trauma better explain a presentation
howToUse: Study by diagnostic category first, then compare similar disorders within the category.
Pay attention to symptom count, duration, and level of impairment.
Practice asking: What diagnosis best explains all of the case details, not just one symptom?
Use the differential diagnosis blocks heavily. That is where many test items are won or lost.
highYieldThemes: A specifier is not a separate diagnosis.
Safety comes first when suicidality, mania, psychosis, or severe substance use is present.

coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.rule: Start with the primary complaint, but do not stop there.
coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.example: A client may present saying 'I have anxiety,' but the full pattern could better fit PTSD, OCD, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, or substance-induced anxiety.

coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.rule: Check duration before committing to a diagnosis.
coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.example: Acute Stress Disorder lasts from 3 days to 1 month after trauma. PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month.

coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.rule: Rule out bipolar disorder before diagnosing unipolar depression when elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, or risky behavior appear.
coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.example: A client with depressive episodes and a history of 4 days of elevated energy and less sleep may meet Bipolar II, not Major Depressive Disorder alone.

coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.rule: Rule out substances, medical causes, and normative responses when appropriate.
coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.example: Intoxication, withdrawal, thyroid issues, grief-related responses, and medication effects can mimic psychiatric disorders.

coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.rule: Use the diagnosis that best accounts for the full pattern and impairment.
coreDiagnosticReasoningRules.example: A client with recurrent intrusive obsessions and compulsions for over an hour a day fits OCD better than GAD, even if both involve anxiety.

diagnosticCategories.title: Depressive Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Depressive disorders are characterized by sadness, loss of interest, cognitive changes, physical symptoms, and impairment. On the exam, they are commonly confused with bipolar disorders, adjustment disorder, grief responses, substance-induced symptoms, and medical conditions.

highYieldDisorders.title: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Major Depressive Disorder is a mood disorder marked by one or more episodes of persistent sadness or loss of interest that lasts at least two weeks and significantly disrupts work, relationships, sleep, appetite, energy, and self-worth. It is more than ordinary sadness — symptoms are pervasive, nearly daily, and represent a clear change from how the person normally functions. MDD can occur as a single episode or recur throughout life, and it carries meaningful suicide risk that must always be assessed.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: At least 5 symptoms during the same 2-week period, with at least one being depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure.
coreCriteria: Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day
Markedly diminished interest or pleasure
Weight or appetite change
Insomnia or hypersomnia
Psychomotor agitation or retardation
Fatigue or loss of energy
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt
Diminished concentration or indecisiveness
Recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, attempt, or plan
highYieldDisorders.minimumThreshold: 5 or more symptoms over 2 weeks, including depressed mood and/or anhedonia
mustRuleOut: Depression due to a medical condition
Normal grief reactions that do not meet full syndrome and impairment

severity.mild: Few symptoms beyond the minimum and minor impairment
severity.moderate: Symptoms and impairment between mild and severe
severity.severe: Many symptoms beyond the minimum and marked impairment

examClues: Daily sadness plus loss of interest is the classic anchor.
The exam often includes fatigue, guilt, poor concentration, sleep disturbance, and passive SI.
If manic or hypomanic history appears anywhere in the case, reconsider MDD.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: MDD is episodic and requires 2 weeks with 5+ symptoms; PDD is chronic depressed mood for at least 2 years with fewer but persistent symptoms.
Adjustment Disorder is tied to an identifiable stressor, begins within 3 months of it, and does not meet full criteria for another disorder.
Bipolar II includes at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode.

miniCase.prompt: A client reports 3 weeks of near-daily sadness, anhedonia, low energy, insomnia, guilt, poor concentration, and thoughts that life is not worth living, with significant work impairment.
miniCase.why: The case exceeds the 2-week threshold, includes more than 5 symptoms, and causes functional impairment.

highYieldDisorders.title: Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia)
highYieldDisorders.description: Persistent Depressive Disorder, formerly called dysthymia, is a chronic, lower-grade form of depression in which a depressed mood is present most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years in adults (one year in children/adolescents). Symptoms are less severe than MDD at any single moment but are far more enduring, often becoming part of how the person sees themselves ('I've always been this way'). Functional impairment accumulates over years of low energy, low self-esteem, and hopelessness.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Chronically depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years.
coreCriteria: Depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for 2 years or more
At least 2 of the following: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness
During the 2-year period, symptoms are not absent for more than 2 months at a time
mustRuleOut: Major depressive episodes only, without chronic baseline depression
examClues: The case often reads as 'I've felt this way for years.'
Chronic low self-esteem and hopelessness are common clues.
Clients may still function, but with longstanding low mood and diminished optimism.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: PDD is chronic, while MDD is episodic. A client can have persistent depression with intermittent major depressive episodes.
Cyclothymia includes alternating hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that do not meet full episode criteria.

highYieldDisorders.title: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder is a childhood diagnosis (onset before age 10, diagnosed between ages 6–18) characterized by severe, recurrent temper outbursts that are grossly out of proportion to the situation, occurring three or more times per week, with a persistently irritable or angry mood between outbursts. It was created to reduce over-diagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder in children with chronic irritability rather than discrete manic episodes.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Severe recurrent temper outbursts with persistent irritability in children and adolescents.
coreCriteria: Severe verbal or behavioral temper outbursts grossly out of proportion to the situation
Outbursts occur 3 or more times per week
Mood between outbursts is persistently irritable or angry
Duration of 12 months or more
Diagnosis between ages 6 and 18, with onset before age 10
mustRuleOut: Oppositional Defiant Disorder as a better explanation when mood syndrome threshold is not met
Autism spectrum-related dysregulation without full DMDD pattern
examClues: Chronic irritability is the key, not episodic mania.
Developed partly to reduce overdiagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder.

highYieldDisorders.title: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
highYieldDisorders.description: PMDD is a cyclical mood disorder in which affective, cognitive, and physical symptoms occur in the final week before menses, improve shortly after onset of menses, and become minimal or absent postmenses. It is clinically significant because symptoms cause distress or impairment and are not simply an exacerbation of another disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Mood lability, irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety tied predictably to the premenstrual phase.
coreCriteria: At least 5 symptoms in most menstrual cycles
At least one core mood symptom: affective lability, irritability/anger, depressed mood, or anxiety/tension
Symptoms improve within a few days after menses begins
Clinically significant distress or impairment
examClues: Timing across the menstrual cycle is the exam clue.

redFlags: Always assess suicidality when depression is present.
Psychotic features change the level of severity and may affect treatment setting.
A history of mania or hypomania changes the diagnostic frame completely.
categoryQuickReview: PDD = 2 years of chronic depressed mood
DMDD = severe irritability and outbursts in youth

diagnosticCategories.title: Anxiety Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Anxiety disorders share fear, anticipation of threat, avoidance, and physiological arousal, but they differ in trigger, symptom pattern, and duration.

highYieldDisorders.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Generalized Anxiety Disorder is characterized by excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple everyday concerns (work, health, finances, family) occurring more days than not for at least six months. The worry is accompanied by physical and cognitive symptoms — restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, and difficulty concentrating — and causes meaningful impairment. Unlike panic disorder, the anxiety is chronic and diffuse rather than episodic.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Excessive anxiety and worry about multiple areas of life occurring more days than not for at least 6 months.
coreCriteria: Excessive anxiety and worry occurring more days than not for 6 months or more
Difficulty controlling the worry
At least 3 of the following in adults: restlessness, fatigue, concentration problems, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance
mustRuleOut: Anxiety better explained by panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, or medical illness
examClues: The worry is broad and chronic, not tied to one object or one social performance setting.
Muscle tension and sleep problems are common clues.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: GAD involves chronic free-floating worry; panic disorder centers on recurrent unexpected panic attacks and fear of future attacks.
OCD obsessions are intrusive, ego-dystonic, and often paired with compulsions. GAD worry feels more like persistent concern.

highYieldDisorders.title: Panic Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Panic Disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks — sudden surges of intense fear or discomfort that peak within minutes and include physical symptoms such as racing heart, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, sweating, trembling, and a sense of impending doom or losing control. To meet criteria, at least one attack must be followed by a month or more of persistent worry about additional attacks, fear of their consequences (e.g., 'having a heart attack,' 'going crazy'), or significant behavior change to avoid them. The attacks come 'out of the blue,' which distinguishes panic disorder from situationally-cued anxiety.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern or maladaptive behavior change related to future attacks.
coreCriteria: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks
At least one month of persistent concern about additional attacks and/or maladaptive behavior changes related to the attacks
examClues: The phrase 'out of the blue' often points to unexpected panic attacks.
Worry about the next attack can lead to avoidance and eventually agoraphobia.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Panic in social anxiety is triggered by scrutiny or evaluation; panic disorder attacks are unexpected.
Agoraphobia is fear/avoidance of places where escape feels difficult; it may occur with or without panic disorder.

highYieldDisorders.title: Social Anxiety Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia) is a persistent, intense fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person may be scrutinized or judged by others — speaking, eating, meeting strangers, performing. The feared situations almost always provoke anxiety, are avoided or endured with distress, and the fear is out of proportion to the actual threat. Symptoms must last six months or more and cause meaningful impairment. A 'performance only' specifier exists for those whose fear is limited to public speaking or performance.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Marked fear of social situations involving possible scrutiny and fear of negative evaluation.
coreCriteria: Marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations where scrutiny is possible
Fear of acting in a way that will be negatively evaluated
Situations almost always provoke fear
Avoidance or endurance with intense anxiety
Persistent, typically 6 months or more
examClues: Fear of embarrassment, judgment, or humiliation is central.
Performance-only subtype often appears in public speaking cases.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Avoidant PD is broader, more pervasive, and personality-based across many contexts.
In social anxiety, the feared consequence is negative evaluation; in panic disorder, it is the attack itself and its implications.

highYieldDisorders.title: Specific Phobia
highYieldDisorders.description: Specific Phobia is a marked, persistent fear of a specific object or situation (animals, heights, blood/injection/injury, flying, enclosed spaces, etc.) that is out of proportion to the actual danger. The phobic stimulus almost always provokes immediate anxiety and is actively avoided or endured with intense distress. Symptoms must last six months or more and impair functioning. Unlike generalized anxiety, the fear is narrowly focused on a clearly identifiable trigger.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation.
coreCriteria: Fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation
Phobic object almost always provokes immediate fear
Active avoidance or endurance with intense anxiety
Fear is out of proportion to actual danger
Persistent, usually 6 months or more
examClues: The trigger is narrow and specific.
Blood-injection-injury type may include vasovagal fainting.

highYieldDisorders.title: Agoraphobia
highYieldDisorders.description: Agoraphobia is marked fear or anxiety about two or more situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like or incapacitating symptoms occur — using public transportation, being in open or enclosed spaces, standing in line or in crowds, or being outside the home alone. These situations are avoided, require a companion, or are endured with intense fear. Symptoms must last six months or more. It can occur with or without panic disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Fear or avoidance of situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like symptoms occur.
coreCriteria: Marked fear or anxiety about 2 or more of the following: public transportation, open spaces, enclosed spaces, lines/crowds, being outside home alone
Situations are avoided because escape might be difficult or help unavailable
Persistent, typically 6 months or more
examClues: The client may become housebound or heavily restricted.
Often linked with but not identical to panic disorder.

highYieldDisorders.title: Separation Anxiety Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Separation Anxiety Disorder involves developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear or anxiety about separation from attachment figures (a parent, partner, or other primary attachment). Symptoms include persistent worry about losing the person or about harm befalling them, refusal to go to school or work, nightmares about separation, and physical complaints when separation is anticipated. Although classically thought of as a childhood disorder, it can occur in adults; duration must be at least four weeks in children and six months in adults.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Developmentally inappropriate fear concerning separation from attachment figures.
coreCriteria: Excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures
Symptoms may include distress on separation, worry about harm to attachment figures, reluctance to be alone, nightmares, physical complaints
examClues: Can occur in adults, not only children.
In adults, the feared attachment figure may be a spouse, child, or partner.

highYieldDisorders.title: Selective Mutism
highYieldDisorders.description: Selective Mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child consistently fails to speak in specific social settings where speaking is expected, despite speaking in other settings. It interferes with school, social communication, or achievement and is not due to lack of language knowledge.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Speaks in some settings but persistently does not speak in expected social settings.
coreCriteria: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations
Speaking occurs in other situations
Interferes with educational, occupational, or social functioning
Duration at least 1 month, not limited to the first month of school
examClues: Child talks normally at home but not at school.

redFlags: Always rule out substance or medical causes when physical anxiety symptoms dominate.
Recurrent panic with chest pain and dizziness may still require medical evaluation.
Avoidance severity helps determine impairment and treatment urgency.
categoryQuickReview: Panic Disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks + future fear
Agoraphobia = avoidance of places where escape feels hard

diagnosticCategories.title: Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders require a stressor or trauma exposure and are differentiated largely by the nature of the event, symptom clusters, and duration.

highYieldDisorders.title: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence — through direct experience, witnessing, learning of a close other's traumatic event, or repeated exposure to aversive details (as in first responders). Symptoms last more than one month and fall into four clusters: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive memories), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked arousal and reactivity (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance). PTSD impairs daily functioning and often co-occurs with depression and substance use.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Symptoms following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, lasting more than 1 month.
traumaExposureWays: learning it occurred to a close other
repeated/extreme indirect exposure to aversive details
examClues: Watch for trauma exposure plus all four symptom domains.
Hypervigilance, nightmares, avoidance, detachment, and startle response are classic clues.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Acute Stress Disorder lasts from 3 days to 1 month after trauma; PTSD lasts longer than 1 month.
Adjustment Disorder follows an identifiable stressor but does not require trauma exposure and does not include the full PTSD syndrome.

miniCase.prompt: A paramedic develops nightmares, intrusive images, hypervigilance, avoidance of ambulance sounds, emotional numbing, and insomnia for 3 months after witnessing a gruesome death.
miniCase.why: The case includes qualifying trauma exposure, the core symptom clusters, and duration longer than 1 month.

highYieldDisorders.title: Acute Stress Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Acute Stress Disorder presents with PTSD-like symptoms — intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal — that begin within days of a traumatic event and last from 3 days to 1 month. If symptoms persist beyond one month, the diagnosis is reconsidered as PTSD. ASD identifies people in the early aftermath of trauma who may benefit from early intervention.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Trauma-related symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the trauma.
coreCriteria: Exposure to trauma
Symptoms from intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal categories
Duration between 3 days and 1 month after trauma
examClues: The timeline is the major clue.
If symptoms last beyond 1 month, reconsider PTSD.

highYieldDisorders.title: Adjustment Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Adjustment Disorder is the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms (depressed mood, anxiety, conduct disturbance) in response to an identifiable stressor — job loss, divorce, illness, relocation — within three months of the stressor's onset. Symptoms cause distress out of proportion to the stressor or significant impairment but do not meet criteria for another mental disorder and are not normal bereavement. Symptoms resolve within six months after the stressor (or its consequences) ends.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor occurring within 3 months of the stressor.
coreCriteria: Symptoms begin within 3 months of the stressor
Distress is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or causes significant impairment
Symptoms do not represent normal bereavement alone and do not meet criteria for another disorder
Once the stressor or its consequences have ended, symptoms do not persist for more than 6 additional months
subtypes: with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct
examClues: Adjustment Disorder is a diagnosis of fit when distress is real and impairing but does not meet full criteria for another syndrome.
The case often features a clear stressor such as divorce, job loss, relocation, or school transition.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: If full depressive syndrome criteria are met, diagnose MDD rather than Adjustment Disorder.
PTSD requires qualifying trauma exposure and specific symptom clusters.

redFlags: Always assess suicide risk in trauma cases, especially when hopelessness, shame, substance use, or sleep disruption are present.
Dissociation and hyperarousal can complicate engagement and treatment planning.
Do not force trauma processing when safety and stabilization are not established.
categoryQuickReview: ASD = trauma + symptoms + 3 days to 1 month
Adjustment Disorder = stressor-linked distress that does not meet another full disorder

diagnosticCategories.title: Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders involve obsessions, compulsions, preoccupations, or repetitive behaviors that are difficult to control and cause distress or impairment.

highYieldDisorders.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder is characterized by obsessions (recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause marked anxiety) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or rigid rules, aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing a feared outcome). The obsessions and compulsions are time-consuming (typically more than one hour per day) or cause significant distress or impairment. The person usually recognizes the thoughts and behaviors as excessive, though insight varies.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Obsessions, compulsions, or both that are time-consuming or cause significant distress/impairment.
coreCriteria: Obsessions: recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause anxiety/distress
Compulsions: repetitive behaviors or mental acts aimed at reducing distress or preventing a feared outcome
The obsessions or compulsions are time-consuming, such as more than 1 hour per day, or cause significant impairment
examClues: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts are key.
The compulsions are meant to neutralize distress, even if they are not realistically connected to the feared event.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: GAD worry is more generalized and experienced as excessive concern; OCD obsessions are intrusive, unwanted, and often bizarre or highly specific.
OCPD traits are ego-syntonic and personality-based; OCD obsessions/compulsions are distressing and unwanted.

miniCase.prompt: A client spends 3 hours daily washing hands and checking locks because they are tormented by intrusive contamination thoughts they know are irrational.
miniCase.why: The case includes intrusive obsessions, compulsive rituals, and significant time consumption.

highYieldDisorders.title: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Body Dysmorphic Disorder involves preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others. The person performs repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing appearance with others) in response to the appearance concerns. The preoccupation causes significant distress or impairment and is not better explained by an eating disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.
coreCriteria: Appearance preoccupation
Repetitive behaviors or mental acts such as mirror checking, comparing, or reassurance seeking
Clinically significant distress or impairment
examClues: The defect is minor or not observable, but the distress is intense.
Time spent checking, hiding, comparing, or seeking reassurance is a clue.

highYieldDisorders.title: Hoarding Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Hoarding Disorder is persistent difficulty discarding or parting with possessions, regardless of their actual value, due to a perceived need to save them and distress associated with discarding. The accumulation results in clutter that congests living areas and substantially compromises their intended use. It causes significant distress or impairment, including unsafe living conditions or family/occupational problems.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of actual value due to a perceived need to save them and distress associated with discarding.
coreCriteria: Persistent difficulty discarding possessions
Perceived need to save items
Distress associated with discarding
Accumulation that congests living areas and compromises intended use
examClues: Living spaces become unusable.
Family conflict and safety issues are common clues.

highYieldDisorders.title: Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder)
highYieldDisorders.description: Trichotillomania involves recurrent pulling out of one’s hair resulting in hair loss, with repeated attempts to decrease or stop the behavior. The behavior may be automatic or focused and often increases with tension or emotional distress.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent hair pulling causing hair loss plus attempts to stop.
coreCriteria: Recurrent hair pulling resulting in hair loss
Repeated attempts to decrease or stop pulling
Distress or impairment
Not attributable to a medical condition or another mental disorder
examClues: Patchy hair loss plus shame or attempts to hide it.

highYieldDisorders.title: Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Excoriation disorder involves recurrent skin picking that causes lesions, with repeated attempts to reduce or stop. It is grouped with OCD-related disorders because the behavior is repetitive and difficult to control.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent skin picking causing lesions plus unsuccessful attempts to stop.
coreCriteria: Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions
Repeated attempts to decrease or stop
Distress or impairment
Not due to substance, medical condition, or another mental disorder
examClues: Look for repeated picking, lesions, and failed stopping attempts.

redFlags: Severe OCD can include significant suicidality due to distress and shame.
Hoarding can create medical and safety risks.
BDD can include suicidality and requests for repeated cosmetic interventions.
categoryQuickReview: OCD = obsessions/compulsions that are distressing and time-consuming
Hoarding = inability to discard + cluttered living spaces

diagnosticCategories.title: Psychotic Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Psychotic disorders are defined by disruptions in reality testing such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms.

highYieldDisorders.title: Schizophrenia
highYieldDisorders.description: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder defined by the presence of two or more characteristic symptoms — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms — for a significant portion of one month, with continuous signs of disturbance lasting at least six months. At least one symptom must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. Functioning in work, relationships, or self-care is markedly below the prior level. Onset is typically in late adolescence or early adulthood.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Two or more core psychotic symptoms for at least 1 month, with continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months and functional decline.
coreCriteria: Two or more of the following for a significant portion of 1 month: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms
At least one must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech
Marked decline in functioning
Continuous signs for at least 6 months
examClues: Negative symptoms and duration help distinguish schizophrenia from brief psychosis.
Functioning below premorbid baseline is important.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Brief psychosis lasts from 1 day to 1 month and returns to premorbid functioning.
Schizoaffective disorder includes a major mood episode plus at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms.

highYieldDisorders.title: Brief Psychotic Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Brief Psychotic Disorder involves the sudden onset of one or more positive psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior) lasting more than one day but less than one month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning. It is often triggered by a marked stressor and is the shortest-duration psychotic diagnosis.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: One or more psychotic symptoms lasting from at least 1 day to less than 1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning.
coreCriteria: One or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior
Duration of at least 1 day but less than 1 month
Full return to premorbid functioning
examClues: Abrupt onset after severe stress may appear.
Duration is the major differentiator.

highYieldDisorders.title: Schizoaffective Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Schizoaffective Disorder is diagnosed when an uninterrupted period of illness includes a major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with the active-phase symptoms of schizophrenia, AND there are delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime of the illness. Mood symptoms are present for the majority of the total illness duration. It bridges the line between schizophrenia and mood disorders.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: An uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode concurrent with schizophrenia symptoms, plus at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms.
coreCriteria: Schizophrenia symptoms present
A major mood episode present for the majority of total illness duration
At least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations without a mood episode
examClues: The psychosis persists even when mood symptoms are absent.
This is what separates it from mood disorder with psychotic features.

highYieldDisorders.title: Schizophreniform Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Schizophreniform disorder has the same core symptom profile as schizophrenia but lasts at least 1 month and less than 6 months. It is often tested as a duration distinction between brief psychotic disorder and schizophrenia.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Schizophrenia-like symptoms lasting 1 to 6 months.
coreCriteria: Two or more psychotic symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, or negative symptoms
At least one symptom is delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech
Episode lasts at least 1 month but less than 6 months
examClues: Duration is the key.

highYieldDisorders.title: Delusional Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Delusional disorder involves one or more delusions lasting at least 1 month without the broader disorganization, negative symptoms, or marked functional decline typical of schizophrenia. Functioning may appear relatively intact outside the delusional belief.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent delusion(s) for at least 1 month with no full schizophrenia picture.
coreCriteria: One or more delusions for 1 month or longer
Criterion A for schizophrenia has never been met
Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from impact of delusion
Behavior is not obviously bizarre or odd outside delusional theme
mustRuleOut: OCD or BDD with absent insight
examClues: A fixed false belief with otherwise organized presentation.

redFlags: Psychosis requires assessment of safety, command hallucinations, ability to care for self, and level of care.
Substances and medical/neurological causes must be considered.
Disorganized behavior and poor insight may increase acute risk.
categoryQuickReview: Schizophrenia = 1 month active symptoms, 6 months total disturbance, functional decline
Brief Psychotic Disorder = 1 day to 1 month
Schizoaffective = mood episode + psychosis alone for 2 weeks at some point

diagnosticCategories.title: Bipolar and Related Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Bipolar disorders include mood elevation, increased energy, and changes in activity level. These disorders are commonly missed when clinicians focus only on depressive episodes.

highYieldDisorders.title: Bipolar I Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Bipolar I Disorder requires at least one lifetime manic episode — a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy lasting at least one week (or any duration if hospitalization is required), accompanied by symptoms such as decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and excessive involvement in risky pleasurable activities. Depressive episodes are common but not required for the diagnosis.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: At least one manic episode, with or without major depressive episodes.
manicEpisodeCriteria: Distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased goal-directed activity or energy
Lasts at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day, or any duration if hospitalization is necessary

At least 3 symptoms (4 if mood is only irritable): grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, more talkative/pressured speech, flight of ideas/racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity/psychomotor agitation, risky behavior
examClues: Decreased need for sleep is a high-yield clue and is not the same as insomnia.
Hospitalization or psychosis automatically suggests full mania, not hypomania.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Bipolar I requires mania. Bipolar II includes hypomania, not mania.
Mood elevation is better explained by intoxication, medication, or another physiological cause.

miniCase.prompt: A client sleeps 2 hours a night for 8 days, becomes grandiose, spends recklessly, talks rapidly, and is hospitalized after becoming severely agitated.
miniCase.why: The case clearly describes a manic episode.

highYieldDisorders.title: Bipolar II Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Bipolar II Disorder requires at least one hypomanic episode (lasting at least four consecutive days, with similar but less severe symptoms than mania, no psychosis, and no marked impairment or hospitalization) AND at least one major depressive episode. The person has never had a full manic episode — that would convert the diagnosis to Bipolar I. Depression is typically the more disabling and presenting feature.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: At least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, with no history of mania.
hypomaniaCriteria: Elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy/activity
At least 3 symptoms (4 if only irritable): grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, more talkative, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased activity, risky behavior
Observable change in functioning, but not severe enough to cause marked impairment or hospitalization
examClues: Clients often present for depression, not hypomania.
A history of brief periods of elevated energy, confidence, less sleep, and increased productivity is a major clue.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: MDD does not include any past hypomanic or manic episode.

highYieldDisorders.title: Cyclothymic Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Cyclothymic Disorder is a chronic mood disorder in which the person experiences numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and numerous periods of depressive symptoms — neither of which fully meet criteria for a hypomanic, manic, or major depressive episode — for at least two years in adults (one year in youth). Symptoms are present at least half the time, with no symptom-free interval longer than two months.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: At least 2 years of numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that never meet full criteria for episodes.
coreCriteria: For at least 2 years, numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and periods of depressive symptoms
Symptoms never meet full criteria for hypomanic episode, manic episode, or major depressive episode
Symptoms present at least half the time and not absent for more than 2 months at a time
examClues: Chronic mood instability without full episodes is the key.
Often mistaken for temperament or personality style.

redFlags: Mania or mixed states can increase suicide risk, impulsivity, and need for higher level of care.
Psychosis during mood elevation signals severity.
Antidepressant history without mood stabilizer may complicate the picture.
categoryQuickReview: Cyclothymia = chronic subthreshold mood swings for 2 years

diagnosticCategories.title: Personality Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Personality disorders are enduring, pervasive, inflexible patterns of inner experience and behavior that deviate from cultural expectations and cause impairment or distress.

highYieldDisorders.title: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Borderline Personality Disorder is a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and emotions, plus marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood. Hallmark features include frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, intense and unstable relationships alternating between idealization and devaluation, identity disturbance, impulsive self-damaging behaviors, recurrent suicidal behavior or self-harm, affective instability, chronic emptiness, intense anger, and stress-related paranoid ideation or dissociation.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Instability in relationships, self-image, affect, and impulse control, often with fear of abandonment and recurrent self-harm or suicidality.
coreFeatures: frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment
examClues: Intense abandonment fear plus self-harm is a major clue.
Relationship instability and rapid shifts in attachment are common.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: BPD mood shifts are often rapid, reactive, and interpersonal; bipolar mood episodes have clearer episode structure and duration.
Trauma may coexist, but the pervasive personality pattern and attachment instability help distinguish BPD.

highYieldDisorders.evidenceBasedTreatment: DBT is the most classically tested evidence-based treatment.

miniCase.prompt: A client alternates between idealizing and devaluing partners, self-harms after perceived rejection, feels chronically empty, and fears abandonment.
miniCase.why: The case centers on instability, self-harm, emptiness, and abandonment sensitivity.

highYieldDisorders.title: Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Antisocial Personality Disorder is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others occurring since age 15, in a person at least 18 years old, with evidence of conduct disorder before age 15. Features include unlawful behavior, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability and aggressiveness, reckless disregard for safety, consistent irresponsibility, and lack of remorse.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Pervasive disregard for and violation of the rights of others since age 15, with diagnosis only at age 18 or older and evidence of conduct disorder before age 15.
coreFeatures: failure to conform to lawful behavior
examClues: History of conduct disorder before age 15 is essential.
The exam may include manipulation, legal issues, aggression, and lack of remorse.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: NPD centers on grandiosity and admiration; ASPD centers on rights violations, exploitation, and rule breaking.

highYieldDisorders.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder is a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency. Unlike OCD, there are no true obsessions or compulsions — the rigidity is ego-syntonic, meaning the person sees their standards and control as appropriate rather than distressing.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and control at the expense of flexibility and efficiency.
coreFeatures: perfectionism that interferes with task completion
difficulty delegating unless others submit exactly
examClues: OCPD is ego-syntonic; the person often sees the style as appropriate.
Differentiate from OCD, where obsessions and compulsions are unwanted and distressing.

highYieldDisorders.title: Paranoid Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Paranoid Personality Disorder is a Cluster A disorder marked by pervasive distrust and suspiciousness such that others’ motives are interpreted as malevolent. The client may be guarded, unforgiving, and preoccupied with doubts about loyalty.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Pervasive distrust and suspicious interpretation of others.
coreCriteria: Suspiciousness without sufficient basis
Doubts loyalty or trustworthiness
Reluctance to confide
Reads hidden threatening meanings into benign events
Bears grudges or perceives attacks
examClues: Distrust is pervasive and personality-based, not a single delusion.

highYieldDisorders.title: Schizoid Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Schizoid Personality Disorder is a Cluster A disorder involving detachment from social relationships and restricted emotional expression. The client often prefers solitary activities and appears indifferent to praise, criticism, or intimacy.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Detached, solitary, emotionally restricted interpersonal style.
coreCriteria: Neither desires nor enjoys close relationships
Almost always chooses solitary activities
Little interest in sexual experiences
Few activities bring pleasure
Lacks close friends
Appears indifferent to praise or criticism
Emotional coldness or flattened affect
examClues: Not anxious avoidance; the person usually does not desire closeness.

highYieldDisorders.title: Schizotypal Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Schizotypal Personality Disorder is a Cluster A disorder marked by social/interpersonal deficits plus cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentric behavior. It may include ideas of reference, odd beliefs, unusual perceptual experiences, and suspiciousness without meeting criteria for a psychotic disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Eccentric behavior plus odd beliefs/perceptions and social deficits.
coreCriteria: Ideas of reference
Odd beliefs or magical thinking
Unusual perceptual experiences
Odd thinking and speech
Suspiciousness
Inappropriate or constricted affect
Odd appearance or behavior
Few close friends
Social anxiety related to paranoid fears
examClues: Magical thinking and eccentricity are key clues.

highYieldDisorders.title: Narcissistic Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Narcissistic Personality Disorder is a Cluster B disorder involving grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy. The client may appear entitled, exploitative, envious, or preoccupied with fantasies of success or power.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Grandiosity, admiration seeking, entitlement, and limited empathy.
coreCriteria: Grandiose sense of self-importance
Fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty, or ideal love
Believes they are special
Requires excessive admiration
Sense of entitlement
Interpersonally exploitative
Lacks empathy
Envious or believes others envy them
Arrogant behaviors or attitudes
examClues: Grandiosity is enduring, not episodic mania.

highYieldDisorders.title: Histrionic Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Histrionic Personality Disorder is a Cluster B disorder marked by excessive emotionality and attention-seeking. Presentation may include dramatic expression, discomfort when not the center of attention, and impressionistic speech.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Pervasive attention-seeking and rapidly shifting, theatrical emotion.
coreCriteria: Uncomfortable when not center of attention
Inappropriately seductive or provocative behavior
Rapidly shifting shallow emotions
Uses appearance to draw attention
Impressionistic speech lacking detail
Dramatic or theatrical expression
Suggestible
Considers relationships more intimate than they are
examClues: Attention-seeking is central.

highYieldDisorders.title: Avoidant Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Avoidant Personality Disorder is a Cluster C disorder involving social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation. Unlike schizoid personality disorder, the person wants connection but avoids it due to fear of rejection or embarrassment.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Wants relationships but avoids them due to fear of criticism or rejection.
coreCriteria: Avoids interpersonal contact due to fear of criticism
Unwilling to get involved unless certain of being liked
Restrained in intimate relationships
Preoccupied with criticism or rejection
Inhibited in new interpersonal situations
Views self as socially inept or inferior
Reluctant to take personal risks
examClues: Desire for closeness differentiates it from schizoid.

highYieldDisorders.title: Dependent Personality Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Dependent Personality Disorder is a Cluster C disorder characterized by an excessive need to be taken care of, leading to submissive/clinging behavior and fears of separation. The person may struggle to make decisions without reassurance and tolerate poor treatment to avoid abandonment.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Excessive need to be cared for with submissive, clingy behavior.
coreCriteria: Difficulty making everyday decisions without reassurance
Needs others to assume responsibility
Difficulty disagreeing due to fear of loss of support
Difficulty initiating projects independently
Goes to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance/support
Feels helpless when alone
Urgently seeks another relationship when one ends
Preoccupied with fears of being left to care for self
examClues: Decision paralysis and need for reassurance are common clues.

redFlags: Self-harm and suicidality are especially important in BPD.
Personality disorder labels should not be applied lightly in early assessment without longitudinal pattern evidence.
Trauma can mimic or coexist with personality pathology.
categoryQuickReview: ASPD = rights violations + conduct disorder before 15

diagnosticCategories.title: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: DSM-5-TR conceptualizes substance disorders on a spectrum of severity rather than the older abuse/dependence split. NCMHCE cases often combine substance use with mood, trauma, legal, or family problems.

highYieldDisorders.title: Substance Use Disorder (General Framework)
highYieldDisorders.description: Substance Use Disorder is a problematic pattern of substance use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, manifested by at least 2 of 11 criteria within a 12-month period across four domains: impaired control (using more than intended, unable to cut down, time spent obtaining/using/recovering, craving), social impairment (failure in roles, social/interpersonal problems, giving up activities), risky use (use in hazardous situations, continued use despite problems), and pharmacological criteria (tolerance, withdrawal). Severity is mild (2–3), moderate (4–5), or severe (6+).
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Problematic pattern of use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, with at least 2 criteria within 12 months.

impairedControl: persistent desire or failed efforts to cut down
great deal of time spent obtaining/using/recovering
socialImpairment: failure to fulfill major role obligations

examClues: The exam often embeds legal, occupational, or relationship consequences.
Craving, failed attempts to cut down, and continued use despite harm are common clues.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: Substance Use Disorder requires clinically significant impairment/distress and threshold criteria.
Sometimes the primary syndrome is induced by the substance rather than independent from it.

miniCase.prompt: A client repeatedly drinks more than planned, has missed work, fights with a spouse about alcohol, has tried to stop several times, and still drinks despite worsening depression.
miniCase.why: The case clearly meets multiple SUD criteria across control, social, and continued-use domains.

redFlags: Withdrawal can be medically dangerous, especially alcohol and sedative withdrawal.
Substance use increases suicide risk and can complicate diagnosis.
Level of care decisions are essential in substance cases.
categoryQuickReview: DSM-5-TR uses one spectrum model: 2+ criteria within 12 months
Always consider intoxication, withdrawal, and substance-induced conditions

diagnosticCategories.title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders begin during the developmental period and affect cognitive, behavioral, social, and academic functioning.

highYieldDisorders.title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development. Several symptoms must be present before age 12, occur in two or more settings (e.g., home and school/work), and cause clear impairment. Three presentations exist: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development.
coreCriteria: At least 6 inattentive symptoms and/or 6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms in children (5+ for older adolescents/adults in many settings)
Several symptoms present before age 12
Symptoms present in 2 or more settings
Clear evidence of impairment
examClues: The two-setting requirement is high yield.
Onset before age 12 is essential.

differentialDiagnosis.keyDifference: ADHD is chronic and developmentally rooted, not only situational or stress-triggered.

highYieldDisorders.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Autism Spectrum Disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder defined by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts (social-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communication, developing/maintaining relationships) AND restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (stereotyped movements, insistence on sameness, highly restricted interests, sensory hyper- or hyporeactivity). Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period and cause clinically significant impairment. Severity is rated at three levels based on support needed.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent deficits in social communication/interaction plus restricted, repetitive behaviors or interests, with onset in the developmental period.
coreCriteria: Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity
Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors
Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships
Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities
examClues: Look for social communication differences plus repetitive behavior patterns or sensory interests.

highYieldDisorders.title: Intellectual Disability
highYieldDisorders.description: Intellectual Disability (Intellectual Developmental Disorder) is characterized by deficits in intellectual functions (reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgment) AND deficits in adaptive functioning (conceptual, social, and practical domains) that limit functioning in one or more activities of daily life. Onset is during the developmental period. Severity (mild, moderate, severe, profound) is determined primarily by adaptive functioning, not IQ alone.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Deficits in intellectual functions and adaptive functioning with onset during the developmental period.
coreCriteria: Deficits in intellectual functioning
Deficits in adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, or practical domains
Onset during development
examClues: Adaptive functioning is central, not IQ alone.

highYieldDisorders.title: Specific Learning Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Specific Learning Disorder involves persistent difficulties learning and using academic skills, such as reading, written expression, or mathematics, despite targeted support. It begins during school-age years and is not explained by intellectual disability, sensory problems, or inadequate instruction.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent impairment in reading, writing, or math despite intervention.
coreCriteria: Academic skill difficulty persists at least 6 months despite targeted help
Affected skills are substantially below age expectations
Begins during school-age years
Not better explained by intellectual disability, sensory deficits, or lack of instruction
examClues: Specify reading, written expression, or mathematics.

highYieldDisorders.title: Tourette’s Disorder / Persistent Tic Disorders
highYieldDisorders.description: Tic disorders involve sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic motor movements or vocalizations. Tourette’s disorder requires both multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for more than one year, with onset before age 18.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Motor and/or vocal tics, with Tourette’s requiring both types for over 1 year.
coreCriteria: Sudden recurrent motor or vocal tics
Tourette’s: multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic
Duration more than 1 year for Tourette’s or persistent tic disorder
Onset before age 18
examClues: Tics are brief, sudden, and nonrhythmic.

highYieldDisorders.title: Communication Disorders
highYieldDisorders.description: Communication disorders include language disorder, speech sound disorder, childhood-onset fluency disorder, and social/pragmatic communication disorder. Exam questions usually test whether communication deficits are better explained by autism spectrum disorder, anxiety, hearing impairment, or language development problems.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent deficits in language, speech, fluency, or social communication.
coreCriteria: Deficits are developmentally inappropriate and impair communication, academics, work, or social participation
Onset in early developmental period
Not better explained by sensory impairment, neurological condition, or intellectual disability alone
examClues: Social pragmatic communication disorder lacks restricted/repetitive behaviors of ASD.

redFlags: Do not confuse trauma, anxiety, language barriers, or educational deprivation with neurodevelopmental disorders without adequate evidence.
Functional impairment and developmental history matter.
categoryQuickReview: ADHD = onset before 12 + symptoms across settings
ASD = social communication deficits + restricted/repetitive patterns
Intellectual Disability = intellectual deficits + adaptive functioning deficits

diagnosticCategories.title: Feeding and Eating Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders involve disturbances in eating behavior and body-related beliefs that create medical, psychological, and functional risk.

highYieldDisorders.title: Anorexia Nervosa
highYieldDisorders.description: Anorexia Nervosa is characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight relative to age, sex, and developmental trajectory; intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain; and disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced (or denial of the seriousness of the low weight). Two subtypes: restricting and binge-eating/purging. Carries the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbance in body image.
coreCriteria: Restriction of intake leading to significantly low body weight
Intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior interfering with weight gain
Disturbance in body image or lack of recognition of seriousness
examClues: Low body weight is required.
Denial of severity is common.

highYieldDisorders.title: Bulimia Nervosa
highYieldDisorders.description: Bulimia Nervosa is defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating (eating an objectively large amount with a sense of loss of control) accompanied by recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (self-induced vomiting, laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise). Binge eating and compensatory behaviors both occur, on average, at least once a week for three months. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. Body weight is typically in the normal or overweight range.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise.
coreCriteria: Recurrent binge eating
Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors
Both occur at least once a week for 3 months
Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight
examClues: Weight may be normal, unlike many anorexia cases.

highYieldDisorders.title: Binge Eating Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Binge Eating Disorder involves recurrent episodes of binge eating (large amount of food, sense of loss of control) at least once a week for three months, associated with marked distress and at least three of: eating rapidly, eating until uncomfortably full, eating large amounts when not hungry, eating alone due to embarrassment, or feeling disgusted/depressed/guilty afterward. Unlike bulimia, there are no regular compensatory behaviors.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent binge eating without regular compensatory behaviors.
coreCriteria: Recurrent binge episodes
Marked distress regarding binge eating
At least once a week for 3 months
No regular compensatory behaviors
examClues: Distinguish from bulimia by the absence of purging/compensation.

highYieldDisorders.title: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)
highYieldDisorders.description: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder is an eating or feeding disturbance — based on lack of interest in eating, sensory avoidance of food characteristics, or fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting) — that results in failure to meet nutritional or energy needs. Consequences include significant weight loss or failure to grow, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or tube feeding, or marked psychosocial impairment. Unlike anorexia, there is no body image disturbance or fear of weight gain.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Restricted intake causing nutritional or psychosocial impairment without body image distortion as the main driver.
examClues: Often related to sensory aversion, fear of choking/vomiting, or low interest in eating, rather than weight/shape concerns.

highYieldDisorders.title: Pica
highYieldDisorders.description: Pica is a feeding and eating disorder involving persistent eating of nonnutritive, nonfood substances such as dirt, paper, paint, hair, or chalk for at least one month. It must be developmentally inappropriate and not culturally sanctioned. It may occur in children, pregnancy, intellectual disability, autism, or other clinical contexts and can create medical risks such as poisoning, obstruction, or infection.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Persistent eating of nonfood substances for at least 1 month.
coreCriteria: Eating nonnutritive, nonfood substances for at least 1 month
Behavior is inappropriate to developmental level
Behavior is not culturally supported or socially normative
If occurring with another disorder or medical condition, it is severe enough to warrant separate clinical attention
examClues: The exam clue is nonfood ingestion plus developmental inappropriateness.

highYieldDisorders.title: Rumination Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Rumination Disorder involves repeated regurgitation of food for at least one month. The food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed, or spit out, and the behavior is not due to a gastrointestinal or medical condition.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Repeated regurgitation of food for at least 1 month.
coreCriteria: Repeated regurgitation of food over at least 1 month
Food may be re-chewed, re-swallowed, or spit out
Not attributable to gastrointestinal or other medical condition
Not occurring exclusively during anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, or ARFID
examClues: Regurgitation, not body-image-driven purging, is central.

redFlags: Medical instability may require urgent referral or higher level of care.
Suicidality, electrolyte problems, and severe malnutrition are high-risk issues.
categoryQuickReview: Anorexia = low weight + fear of weight gain + body image disturbance
ARFID = restrictive intake without body image focus

diagnosticCategories.title: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders involve distressing somatic symptoms and/or excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to health concerns.

highYieldDisorders.title: Somatic Symptom Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Somatic Symptom Disorder involves one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or disrupt daily life, accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the symptoms — disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of symptoms, persistently high anxiety about health, or excessive time and energy devoted to them. The state of being symptomatic is persistent (typically more than six months). The symptoms themselves may or may not be medically explained — what matters is the disproportionate response to them.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: One or more distressing somatic symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to those symptoms.
coreCriteria: One or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or disruptive
Excessive thoughts, anxiety, or time/energy devoted to health concerns
Persistence, typically more than 6 months
examClues: The symptoms may or may not be medically explained. The key is the excessive psychological response.

highYieldDisorders.title: Illness Anxiety Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Illness Anxiety Disorder involves preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness despite absent or mild somatic symptoms. Health anxiety remains high even after reassurance, and the person either excessively checks health status or avoids medical care.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: High illness preoccupation with minimal or no somatic symptoms.
coreCriteria: Preoccupation with having/acquiring serious illness
Somatic symptoms absent or mild
High anxiety about health
Excessive health behaviors or maladaptive avoidance
Illness preoccupation present at least 6 months
examClues: If symptoms are minimal but illness fear is high, think illness anxiety.

highYieldDisorders.title: Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder)
highYieldDisorders.description: Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder involves neurological-like symptoms such as weakness, paralysis, seizures, sensory loss, or abnormal movement that are incompatible with recognized neurological or medical conditions. Symptoms are real to the client and cause distress or impairment.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Neurological symptoms inconsistent with medical disease patterns.
coreCriteria: One or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function
Clinical findings show incompatibility with recognized neurological or medical conditions
Not better explained by another medical or mental disorder
Causes distress, impairment, or warrants evaluation
examClues: Do not imply the client is faking; symptoms are not intentionally produced.

highYieldDisorders.title: Factitious Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Factitious Disorder involves falsification of physical or psychological symptoms, or induction of injury/disease, without obvious external rewards. The motivation is to assume the sick role, which differentiates it from malingering.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Intentional symptom falsification without clear external reward.
coreCriteria: Falsification of symptoms or induction of illness/injury
Presents self or another as ill, impaired, or injured
Deceptive behavior occurs without obvious external rewards
examClues: No obvious external incentive = factitious; external gain = malingering.

redFlags: Do not assume symptoms are 'all psychological.' Medical evaluation may still be needed.
Validate distress while avoiding reinforcement of endless reassurance cycles.
categoryQuickReview: Somatic Symptom Disorder = distressing symptoms + excessive health-related thoughts/behaviors

diagnosticCategories.title: Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: These disorders involve problems with emotional and behavioral self-control and often appear in child/adolescent cases.

highYieldDisorders.title: Conduct Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Conduct Disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms or rules are violated, evidenced by at least 3 of 15 criteria over the past 12 months across four categories: aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious violations of rules. It is diagnosed in those under 18 (those over 18 would warrant Antisocial Personality Disorder consideration). Childhood-onset (before age 10) carries a worse prognosis than adolescent-onset.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Repetitive and persistent pattern of violating rights of others or major age-appropriate norms/rules.
examClues: A history of conduct disorder before age 15 is necessary for later ASPD diagnosis.

highYieldDisorders.title: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)
highYieldDisorders.description: Oppositional Defiant Disorder is a childhood/adolescent disorder involving a persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness toward authority figures. It does not include the serious violation of rights or major societal rules seen in conduct disorder.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Angry, defiant, argumentative pattern toward authority for at least 6 months.
coreCriteria: Angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness
At least 4 symptoms for at least 6 months
Occurs with at least one non-sibling individual
Causes distress or impairment in the individual or others
examClues: ODD = defiance; conduct disorder = rights/rules violations.

highYieldDisorders.title: Intermittent Explosive Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Intermittent Explosive Disorder involves recurrent behavioral outbursts representing failure to control aggressive impulses. Outbursts are disproportionate to the provocation, impulsive rather than premeditated, and not committed for a tangible objective.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent disproportionate aggressive outbursts.
coreCriteria: Recurrent verbal or physical aggression out of proportion to stressor
Outbursts are impulsive/anger-based, not premeditated
Not done to achieve money, power, intimidation, or other tangible goal
Causes distress, impairment, or legal/financial consequences
examClues: Impulsive explosive anger differentiates it from planned aggression.

highYieldDisorders.title: Kleptomania
highYieldDisorders.description: Kleptomania involves recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or monetary value. Tension increases before the theft and relief or gratification follows.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Impulse-driven stealing of unneeded items with tension before and relief after.
coreCriteria: Recurrent failure to resist stealing items not needed for use or value
Increasing tension before theft
Pleasure, gratification, or relief during theft
Not committed out of anger, vengeance, delusion, or hallucination
examClues: Stealing is not for practical gain.

highYieldDisorders.title: Pyromania
highYieldDisorders.description: Pyromania involves deliberate and purposeful fire setting on more than one occasion, with tension before the act and fascination, pleasure, or relief related to fire. It is not diagnosed when fire setting is for financial gain, revenge, ideology, concealment of crime, or impaired judgment from substances/mania/psychosis.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Purposeful fire setting with fascination and relief, not external gain.
coreCriteria: Deliberate fire setting more than once
Tension or arousal before the act
Fascination with fire and its contexts
Pleasure, gratification, or relief when setting or witnessing fires
Not for external reward, ideology, revenge, concealment, or impaired judgment
examClues: Ask why the fire was set. External motive rules out pyromania.

redFlags: Assess safety, aggression, cruelty, fire-setting, and legal problems.
Family environment, trauma, and neurodevelopmental issues may complicate the picture.
categoryQuickReview: Conduct Disorder matters partly because it is a prerequisite history for ASPD.

diagnosticCategories.title: Dissociative Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Dissociative disorders involve disruption in consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control, or behavior, often associated with trauma or severe stress.

highYieldDisorders.title: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID)
highYieldDisorders.description: DID involves disruption of identity with two or more distinct personality states or possession experiences, along with recurrent gaps in recall. It is associated with severe trauma histories but must be distinguished from psychosis, malingering, substances, and culturally normative possession practices.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Two or more identity states plus recurrent memory gaps.
coreCriteria: Disruption of identity with two or more distinct personality states
Recurrent gaps in recall of everyday events, personal information, or traumatic events
Distress or impairment
Not a normal part of cultural/religious practice
Not attributable to substances or medical condition
examClues: Memory gaps and identity discontinuity are central.

highYieldDisorders.title: Dissociative Amnesia
highYieldDisorders.description: Dissociative Amnesia involves inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually traumatic or stressful, that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. It may occur with dissociative fugue, involving purposeful travel or bewildered wandering.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Trauma-related autobiographical memory gaps beyond ordinary forgetting.
coreCriteria: Inability to recall important autobiographical information
Usually traumatic or stressful in nature
Inconsistent with ordinary forgetting
Distress or impairment
examClues: May include fugue: travel/wandering with amnesia.

highYieldDisorders.title: Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: This disorder involves persistent or recurrent depersonalization, derealization, or both, while reality testing remains intact. Clients may feel detached from their body, thoughts, emotions, or surroundings, but they know the experience is unusual rather than literally true.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Detachment from self or surroundings with intact reality testing.
coreCriteria: Persistent or recurrent depersonalization and/or derealization
Reality testing remains intact
Distress or impairment
Not due to substances, medical condition, panic attacks alone, PTSD, or psychosis
examClues: Intact reality testing distinguishes it from psychosis.

diagnosticCategories.title: Elimination Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Elimination disorders are primarily childhood diagnoses involving inappropriate elimination after the developmental age when continence is expected.

highYieldDisorders.title: Enuresis
highYieldDisorders.description: Enuresis involves repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes, whether involuntary or intentional, after the child has reached a developmental age when bladder control is expected.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Repeated urination into bed/clothes after age 5.
coreCriteria: Repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes
At least twice weekly for 3 months or causes distress/impairment
Chronological or developmental age at least 5 years
Not due to substance or medical condition
examClues: Age 5 is the key developmental cutoff.

highYieldDisorders.title: Encopresis
highYieldDisorders.description: Encopresis involves repeated passage of feces into inappropriate places after the child is developmentally expected to have bowel control. It may occur with constipation and overflow incontinence or without constipation.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Repeated feces passage into inappropriate places after age 4.
coreCriteria: Repeated passage of feces into inappropriate places
At least once per month for 3 months
Chronological or developmental age at least 4 years
Not due to substance or medical condition except constipation mechanism
examClues: Age 4 cutoff; specify with or without constipation.

diagnosticCategories.title: Sleep-Wake Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Sleep-wake disorders are tested mainly through recognition and rule-out reasoning, especially when sleep problems mimic mood, anxiety, trauma, substance, or medical disorders.

highYieldDisorders.title: Insomnia Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Insomnia Disorder involves dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality due to difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or early-morning awakening, despite adequate opportunity for sleep. It causes distress or impairment and occurs at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least 3 nights/week for 3 months.
coreCriteria: Sleep difficulty despite adequate opportunity
At least 3 nights per week
At least 3 months
Distress or impairment
examClues: Do not diagnose as primary if another condition better explains it.

highYieldDisorders.title: Narcolepsy
highYieldDisorders.description: Narcolepsy involves recurrent periods of an irrepressible need to sleep or lapses into sleep, with features such as cataplexy, hypocretin deficiency, or REM sleep abnormalities.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Recurrent irresistible sleep attacks with cataplexy or REM-related evidence.
coreCriteria: Recurrent need to sleep or lapses into sleep at least 3 times per week for 3 months
Cataplexy, hypocretin deficiency, or REM sleep latency findings may support diagnosis
examClues: Cataplexy is sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion.

highYieldDisorders.title: Nightmare Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Nightmare Disorder involves repeated extended dysphoric dreams that are well remembered and usually involve threats to survival, security, or physical integrity. On awakening, the person is rapidly oriented and alert.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Repeated distressing remembered dreams with rapid orientation on awakening.
coreCriteria: Repeated dysphoric dreams involving threat
Rapid orientation and alertness after awakening
Distress or impairment
Not due to substances or another disorder alone
examClues: Sleep terrors involve confusion and poor recall; nightmares are remembered.

diagnosticCategories.title: Neurocognitive Disorders
diagnosticCategories.overview: Neurocognitive disorders involve acquired cognitive decline and are tested through differential diagnosis with depression, delirium, substance effects, and normal aging.

highYieldDisorders.title: Delirium
highYieldDisorders.description: Delirium is an acute disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition that develops over a short period and tends to fluctuate. It is a medical priority, not a counseling diagnosis to treat with routine psychotherapy alone.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Acute fluctuating confusion with impaired attention/awareness.
coreCriteria: Disturbance in attention and awareness
