Develops over hours to days and fluctuates
Additional cognitive disturbance such as memory, language, perception, or orientation changes
Evidence of medical, substance, or multiple causes
examClues: Acute onset + fluctuating attention = medical referral/urgent evaluation.

highYieldDisorders.title: Major Neurocognitive Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Major Neurocognitive Disorder involves significant cognitive decline from a previous level in one or more domains and interference with independence in everyday activities. Etiologies may include Alzheimer’s disease, vascular disease, traumatic brain injury, substance/medication causes, and others.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Significant acquired cognitive decline that interferes with independence.
coreCriteria: Significant cognitive decline from previous performance
Deficits interfere with independence in everyday activities
Not exclusively during delirium
Not better explained by another mental disorder
examClues: Functional independence is the major vs mild distinction.

highYieldDisorders.title: Mild Neurocognitive Disorder
highYieldDisorders.description: Mild Neurocognitive Disorder involves modest cognitive decline that does not interfere with independence, though greater effort, compensatory strategies, or accommodations may be needed.
highYieldDisorders.hallmark: Modest acquired cognitive decline without loss of independence.
coreCriteria: Modest cognitive decline from previous level
Independence in everyday activities is preserved
May require more effort or compensatory strategies
Not exclusively during delirium
examClues: Independence remains intact.

rows.anchor: 5+ symptoms including depressed mood and/or anhedonia
chronic depressed mood with at least 2 associated symptoms
rows.commonTrap: Confusing chronic baseline depression with recurrent episodes only

rows.anchor: stressor-linked distress that does not meet another full syndrome
rows.commonTrap: Using it when full MDD criteria are already met

rows.anchor: impairing stress response without full trauma syndrome
no history of mania or hypomania
at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode
2 years of subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms

commonExamTraps: Diagnosing depression without screening for mania/hypomania history
Choosing Adjustment Disorder when full criteria for another diagnosis are met
Confusing PTSD with Acute Stress Disorder because the symptom pattern is similar but the timeline differs
Confusing OCD obsessions with generalized worry
Overlooking conduct disorder history before diagnosing ASPD
Treating a specifier such as 'with anxious distress' as though it were the primary diagnosis
Ignoring substances, medical conditions, or medication effects

redFlagAlerts.title: Suicidality
redFlagAlerts.clinicalPriority: Risk assessment comes before routine diagnostic refinement when acute safety concerns are present.

redFlagAlerts.title: Mania/Psychosis
redFlagAlerts.clinicalPriority: These symptoms may indicate bipolar spectrum illness, psychotic disorder, substance effect, or need for higher level of care.

redFlagAlerts.title: Substance/Medical Rule-Out
redFlagAlerts.clinicalPriority: Do not lock into a primary psychiatric diagnosis without considering physiological causes.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client has 8 months of constant worry about finances, family, work, and health, with muscle tension, insomnia, fatigue, and irritability.
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Broad worry across domains for more than 6 months with associated symptoms.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client develops nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbing, and hypervigilance for 2 weeks after a violent assault.
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Post-trauma syndrome present within the 3-day to 1-month window.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client reports 2 years of chronic low mood, hopelessness, low energy, and low self-esteem, without symptom-free periods longer than 2 months.
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Chronic depressive baseline exceeding the 2-year threshold.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client experiences repeated intrusive contamination thoughts and spends hours cleaning to reduce distress despite knowing the fear is excessive.
miniCaseDrills.rationale: Intrusive obsessions plus compulsive rituals that are time-consuming.

miniCaseDrills.case: A client presents for depression but also reports several past periods of 5 days of little sleep, unusually high confidence, increased goal-directed activity, and excessive spending, with no hospitalization.
miniCaseDrills.rationale: History suggests hypomania plus depression rather than unipolar depression.

memoryHooks: Panic Disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks
PTSD = trauma + 4 symptom cluster pattern + >1 month
ASD = trauma symptoms in the first month
finalTakeaways: The best diagnosis is the one that explains the whole pattern, not just the loudest symptom.
Duration, impairment, and exclusions often decide the answer.
When two diagnoses seem possible, ask which one the vignette supports more completely.

checkpointQuestions.question: A client has intrusive trauma memories, avoidance, hypervigilance, and sleep disturbance for 10 days after a carjacking. What diagnosis best fits?
A client has chronic depressed mood for years with low self-esteem and hopelessness, but no symptom-free period longer than 2 months. What diagnosis best fits?
A client is terrified of being judged while eating in public and avoids restaurants for that reason. What diagnosis best fits?

A client has one major depressive episode and also a past 4-day period of elevated mood, less sleep, more talkativeness, and increased productivity without hospitalization. What diagnosis should be strongly considered?
A client worries excessively about work, family, finances, and health for 7 months and cannot control the worry. What diagnosis best fits?

sourceBasis: Coverage is based on DSM-5-TR diagnostic categories and NCMHCE-style counseling exam relevance. It is an exam-prep reference, not a replacement for the DSM-5-TR text or supervised diagnosis.
